explain.say: Today we are learning about composition rules in art.
The rule of thirds suggests dividing your picture into nine equal parts.
Try placing your main subject along these imaginary lines or at the intersections.

draw.text: Place subjects on lines or intersections

explain.say: Leading lines are visual paths that guide the viewer's eye through the art.

draw.text: Leading Lines: Guide the viewer's eye

explain.say: Look for natural lines like rivers, roads, or fences to draw the eye.
In everyday life, when you photograph a sunset, use the rule of thirds.

faq.q: Does the rule of thirds mean I cannot put my subject in the center?
faq.a: No, it is a guideline, not a strict rule to follow always. You can center things if you want a very direct, symmetrical look.

faq.q: What kind of lines work best as leading lines?
faq.a: Any strong, visible line works well, such as paths, railings, or even rows of trees. The line should naturally point towards something important.
asks: What makes a good leading line?
Do lines have to be straight?

faq.q: If I use both rules, do they fight each other?
faq.a: No, they can work together very well to strengthen your composition. Use the lines to place your subject correctly on the thirds.
No, these principles apply to drawing, painting, and even designing posters. Composition is about arrangement.

faq.q: What if my picture is very busy?
faq.a: If the picture is busy, use leading lines to simplify it by guiding the viewer to one main point. This helps reduce visual clutter.
asks: How do I simplify a complex image?
What if there is too much stuff?

facts: The rule of thirds divides an image into nine equal sections.
Placing key elements on the intersections often creates visual interest.
Leading lines direct the viewer's gaze towards a focal point.
These rules help create a more balanced and engaging composition.

quiz.say: If you place the most important part of your picture on one of the four corners created by the thirds grid, which rule are you using?
quiz.why: This placement uses the grid intersections to balance the image.

wrong.1: Leading lines describe paths, not specific points on a grid.
wrong.2: Focal point is what you are trying to achieve, not the rule itself.
wrong.3: Symmetry means mirroring, which is different from using the thirds grid.

quiz.say: A winding path in a photograph that starts in the foreground and moves toward a distant building is an example of:
quiz.why: The path acts as a visual guide, leading your eye to the building.

wrong.0: The path is unlikely to be perfectly mirrored on both sides.
wrong.2: This describes a path, not the division of the image into thirds.
wrong.3: This is too general; leading lines describe the specific element.

quiz.say: To make a picture feel balanced using the rule of thirds, you might place a large object on one side and balance it with:

options.show: A smaller object on the opposite third
options.say: A smaller object on the opposite third

quiz.why: You balance weight by placing visual interest on the opposing third line.

wrong.1: Putting everything in the center often makes the image feel heavy and static.
wrong.2: While lines help, they are about direction, not necessarily balancing weight.
wrong.3: Color or size is better for balancing weight than just darkness.
